title: Attributing a suggestion's effect on the next decision from exposure and outcome logs
when: Use when a recommendation trial logs per-suggestion exposure with event IDs and timestamps, and per-prompt outcomes exist for an assigned set. Do not use it to claim causal help when the exposed group is self-selected and too small to compare against the rest.
found: The dashboard cannot establish that reading a suggestion helped the next decision. Only 2 of the 5 selected suggestions were exposed before the assistant acted, 1 arrived after the action, and 2 were dropped. Outcomes exist for all 200 assigned prompts, but the dashboard does not link those outcomes to the exposure events, and the selected reads are self-chosen rather than randomly assigned.
how: 1) Join each exposure event to its prompt via event ID and keep only exposures whose timestamp precedes the assistant's action; label the rest as after-action or dropped. 2) Define the comparison on assigned arm, not on selected reads (intent-to-treat): compare outcomes for all prompts assigned to the suggestion arm against control, whether or not the suggestion was read. 3) Report the exposed-before-action count and its confidence interval alongside the outcome difference. 4) Only call the effect helpful if the assignment was randomized, the outcome is defined before the join, and the difference holds beyond chance; otherwise report it as descriptive only.
evidence: Dashboard: 200 assigned prompts, 5 suggestions selected. Event IDs: 2 selected suggestions reached the assistant before its action, 1 after acting, 2 dropped (2+1+2=5). Outcomes recorded for all 200 prompts. Only 2 exposures precede any decision, which is too few to separate a suggestion effect from noise or selection.
